previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension, was admitted with worsening right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the right lower quadrant and retrosternal chest pain. He had vomited twice and reported a fall four days prior with brief loss of consciousness. In the ED, he was hypotensive with a systolic blood pressure in the 70s, requiring fluid resuscitation. Workup revealed acute kidney injury likely due to prerenal causes, which improved with IV fluids. CT imaging showed mesenteric stranding suggestive of mesenteritis, fatty liver, trace ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions with right predominance. His cardiac evaluation was notable for new T-wave inversions on EKG, but serial troponins were negative. A nuclear stress test revealed normal perfusion but severely reduced ejection fraction of 16%, indicating possible alcohol- or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. He displayed signs of alcohol withdrawal and was managed with CIWA protocol, thiamine, and multivitamins. Despite medical recommendations, he left the hospital against medical advice immediately after completing the stress test, declining further evaluation and discharge instructions.

fibrillation with RVR, and systolic heart failure who presented 
with chest pain, abdominal pain, and intoxication with recent 
PMIBI with evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy and significantly 
impaired systolic function (EF 16%). Patient ruled out for MI. A 
TTE revealed an EF of 35%. His cardiomyopathy was attributed to 
his tachyarrhythmia. His calcium channel blocker was 
discontinued given his heart failure. He was started on 
Metoprolol with rates persistently in the 110s-140s at rest, 
with rates to 160s with exertion. Metoprolol was titrated to 
succinate 200 mg PO daily. Digoxin was started as he showed some 
improvement in his rates, resting heart rate was more 
consistently in the 110s. He CHADS2 score is 1. He was continued 
on ASA and it was felt that he was a poor candidate for Coumadin 
given his poor nutritional status and current social situation. 
He was started on low-dose Lisinopril with plans to add on 
Spironolactone. Psychiatry was consulted on admission as there 
had been a question of Section 35 on prior admission. As the 
patient was initially cooperative with the primary team's plan, 
it was not felt that there was much that could be offered. On 
the fourth day of his hospitalization, the patient became 
suddenly demanded to be dishcarged from the hospital. He 
repeatedly stated that he ""would be fine"" and that there ""was 
nothing wrong with [my] heart."" A code purple was called when 
the patient became agitated and tried to leave. Psychiatry 
evaluated the patient and felt that he had capacity to leave. 
Further discussion revealed that a Section 35 could not be 
instituted quickly and often takes weeks to months to acheive. 
Patient was given prescriptions for his Metoprolol, Digoxing, 
Lisinopril and Aspirin, but eloped before he could sign the AMA 
form. 
. 
Other Issues by Problem:
.  
#. Abdominal Pain: CT scan on last admission (<1 week ago) found 
mesenteritis with possible etiologies considered including 
malignancy, TB, HIV, and nutritional deficiency all of which 
were excluded except TB. His pain, however, was likely related 
to an esophageal/peptic source given his high risk behavior, 
hematemesis, and heart burn symptoms. Acute pancreatitis 
unlikely given negative lipase though chronic pancreatitis is 
possible. GI was consulted on last admission and did recommend 
EGD, however, wanted cardiac work up first and as above this 
issue has not been resolved. Patient was not able to be 
stabilized from a cardiac standpoint, so this was not pursued. 
Patient was continued on his home Omeprazole throughout 
admission. 
. 
#. Hypertension: Patient was normotensive on admission. He had 
diastolic hypertension at times throughout admission. He was on 
Metoprolol and Lisinopril as above. 
.  
#. EtOH Intoxication: Blood alcohol on arrival of 484. History 
of regular heavy drinking placed patient at high risk for 
withdrawal. Patient received banana bag in ED. EtOH abuse 
appeared to be impairing his ability to care for himself. 
Patient showed no overt evidence of withdrawal but was kept on a 
CIWA throughout admission. When his heart rate did not initially 
respond to Metoprolol and Digoxin, he received Diazepam for 
possible withdrawal with no change in his heart rate. He 
received Thiamine, Folate and an MVI throughout admission. 
.  
#. Liver Enzyme Elevation: Likely due to EtOH abuse. Patient 
with EtOH abuse and AST/ALT : 91/38 in classic EtOH hepatitis 
pattern on admission. Hepatitis serologies negative on last 
admission and RUQ u/s shows fatty liver c/w ETOH. Liver enzymes 
trended down prior to admission.
